title: Transcendence of Lacunary Sums
description: A problem about the transcendence of infinite series with lacunary (rapidly growing) exponents. Erdős proved transcendence under strong growth conditions, but the general conjecture remains open.

meta.author: Paul Erdős

mathlibDependencies.description: Predicate for transcendence over a field (element is not algebraic)
Infinite series summation as a topological limit of partial sums
Factorial function and basic lemmas including factorial_lt_of_lt

references.citation: Erdős, P. (1975). Some problems and results on the irrationality of the sum of infinite series. J. Math. Sci., 10:1-7.
Erdős, P. (1988). On the irrationality of certain series: problems and results. In: New Advances in Transcendence Theory, Cambridge Univ. Press, pp. 102-109.
Liouville, J. (1844). Sur des classes très étendues de quantités dont la valeur n'est ni algébrique ni même réductible à des irrationelles algébriques. C. R. Acad. Sci. Paris, 18:883-885.

originalContributions: Formal definition of lacunarySum as tsum over 1/2^{n_k}
Definition of HasWeakGrowth (lim sup n_k/k = infinity) and HasStrongGrowth (superpolynomial growth)
Formal statement of the open Erdos Problem #247 conjecture
Axiomatization of Erdos's 1975 transcendence theorem for superpolynomial growth
Proofs of strict monotonicity for factorial, exponential, and quadratic index sequences
Axiomatization of superpolynomial growth for k! and 2^k
Derived transcendence of Sigma 1/2^{k!} and Sigma 1/2^{2^k} from the main axiom
Explicit construction of the open case: squareSeq and square_sum for n_k = k^2
Summary theorem packaging the three main results

overview.historicalContext: The study of transcendental numbers began with Liouville's 1844 construction of the first explicit transcendental, the Liouville constant L = sum 10^{-k!}, which is transcendental precisely because factorial growth makes it approximable by rationals far better than any algebraic number allows. Hermite (1873) proved e transcendental and Lindemann (1882) proved pi transcendental, but these results relied on special properties of exponential functions rather than approximation arguments. Erdos returned to Liouville-type methods in 1975, proving that the lacunary sum sum 1/2^{n_k} is transcendental whenever the sequence n_k grows faster than any polynomial (superpolynomial growth). His proof generalizes Liouville's insight: truncating the sum at the K-th term gives a rational p/q with q = 2^{n_K}, and when n_k grows superpolynomially, the tail sum is smaller than c/q^d for any fixed algebraic degree d. The full conjecture, that mere faster-than-linear growth (lim sup n_k/k = infinity) suffices, remains open. Erdos noted in 1988 that these problems 'seem hopeless at present.' The simplest open case is n_k = k^2, where the sum sum 1/2^{k^2} (related to the Jacobi theta function theta_3) resists all known techniques.
overview.problemStatement: Let n_1 < n_2 < ... be a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers such that lim sup n_k/k = infinity. Is the sum S = sum_{k=1}^{infinity} 1/2^{n_k} necessarily transcendental? Erdos (1975) proved YES under the stronger condition that lim sup n_k/k^t = infinity for ALL t >= 1 (superpolynomial growth). The general conjecture for merely faster-than-linear growth remains open.
overview.proofStrategy: The formalization axiomatizes Erdos's 1975 theorem and derives concrete corollaries. The lacunary sum is defined using Mathlib's tsum (topological sum). Two growth conditions are defined: HasWeakGrowth (for all C, exists k with n_k > C*k) captures faster-than-linear growth, and HasStrongGrowth (for all polynomial degree t and constant C, exists k with n_k > C*k^t) captures superpolynomial growth. The main axiom erdos_transcendence_strong asserts transcendence under strong growth plus strict monotonicity. Three example sequences are examined: k! and 2^k satisfy strong growth (axiomatized), yielding transcendence corollaries proved by direct application of the main axiom. The quadratic sequence k^2 satisfies only weak growth, illustrating the open gap. A summary theorem packages the three main results.
keyInsights: The sum S = sum 1/2^{n_k} is a binary number with 1s at positions n_k; its transcendence depends on how sparsely these 1s are distributed
Liouville's approximation theorem provides the key tool: if alpha is algebraic of degree d, then |alpha - p/q| > c/q^d, bounding how well rationals can approximate alpha
Truncating the lacunary sum at term K gives rational p_K/2^{n_K} with error sum_{j>K} 1/2^{n_j} < 1/2^{n_{K+1}-1}; superpolynomial growth makes this error smaller than any Liouville bound
The gap between weak growth (faster than linear) and strong growth (faster than any polynomial) is where the difficulty concentrates; even quadratic growth n_k = k^2 is open
The Liouville constant sum 10^{-k!} is the classical ancestor of these lacunary transcendence results, using factorial growth to achieve approximation quality exceeding any algebraic degree

sections.title: Part I: The Lacunary Sum
sections.summary: Defines lacunarySum (n : N -> N) : R as the topological sum tsum (fun k => 1/2^{n k}). This is the central object of the problem: an infinite binary expansion with 1s at positions determined by the sequence n. The 'lacunary' (gappy) character emerges when n_k grows fast, making the 1s increasingly sparse.

sections.title: Part II: Growth Conditions
sections.summary: Defines two growth conditions on the index sequence. HasWeakGrowth requires that for all C > 0, there exists k > 0 with n_k > C*k, equivalent to lim sup n_k/k = infinity (faster-than-linear growth). HasStrongGrowth strengthens this to require n_k > C*k^t for ALL polynomial degrees t >= 1 and all constants C > 0, meaning the sequence outgrows every polynomial (superpolynomial growth).

sections.title: Part III: The Main Conjecture (OPEN)
sections.summary: Defines erdos_247_conjecture as a Prop: for all strictly increasing n with HasWeakGrowth, the lacunary sum is Transcendental over Q. This is the full open conjecture. The formalization uses Mathlib's Transcendental predicate and StrictMono to state it precisely.

sections.title: Part IV: Erdos's Partial Result (1975)
sections.summary: Axiomatizes erdos_transcendence_strong: for strictly increasing n with HasStrongGrowth, the lacunary sum is transcendental. This is Erdos's 1975 theorem, the strongest known result toward the full conjecture. The doc comment outlines the Liouville-type proof: algebraic numbers of degree d satisfy |alpha - p/q| > c/q^d, but superpolynomial growth in n_k produces rational approximations violating this bound for every d.

sections.title: Part V: Examples
sections.summary: Provides two concrete applications. First proves factorial_strictMono (k -> (k+1)! is StrictMono) and pow2_strictMono (k -> 2^k is StrictMono) using Mathlib's factorial_lt_of_lt and pow_lt_pow_right. Then axiomatizes factorial_strong_growth and pow2_strong_growth (both k! and 2^k outgrow every polynomial). Finally derives factorial_sum_transcendental (sum 1/2^{k!} is transcendental) and pow2_sum_transcendental (sum 1/2^{2^k} is transcendental) by direct application of erdos_transcendence_strong.

sections.title: Part VI: The Gap Between Conditions
sections.summary: Examines squareSeq (k -> (k+1)^2) as the canonical example in the gap between weak and strong growth. Proves square_strictMono via Nat.pow_lt_pow_left. Defines square_sum := lacunarySum squareSeq. The sum sum 1/2^{k^2} satisfies weak growth but not strong growth, so Erdos's theorem does not apply. Whether this sum is transcendental remains open.

sections.title: Part VII: Summary
sections.summary: Packages the main results as problem_247_summary: a conjunction of (1) Erdos's theorem for strong growth, (2) transcendence of the factorial sum, and (3) transcendence of the double-exponential sum. Proved via exact \<erdos_transcendence_strong, factorial_sum_transcendental, pow2_sum_transcendental\>. The file ends with #check commands for the conjecture and theorem.

conclusion.summary: This formalization captures Erdos Problem #247 on the transcendence of lacunary sums sum 1/2^{n_k}. The central objects are two growth conditions (faster-than-linear vs superpolynomial) and the lacunary sum defined via tsum. Erdos's 1975 theorem, axiomatized here, establishes transcendence under superpolynomial growth using Liouville-type approximation arguments. Two concrete transcendence results (for k! and 2^k index sequences) are derived as corollaries. The quadratic sequence k^2 illustrates the open gap.
conclusion.implications: If the full conjecture were proved, it would establish that any infinite binary number with 1s growing faster than linearly sparse must be transcendental. This would provide a clean characterization linking the arithmetic complexity (algebraic vs transcendental) of a real number to the combinatorial sparseness of its binary representation. The open case n_k = k^2 connects to the theory of theta functions and modular forms, since sum q^{k^2} is essentially a Jacobi theta function.
openQuestions: Is sum 1/2^{k^2} transcendental? (The simplest open case, connected to Jacobi theta functions)
Can we at least prove sum 1/2^{k^2} is irrational, or not a root of any polynomial of degree <= d?
What is the exact growth threshold: how slowly can n_k grow while still guaranteeing transcendence?
Does the base matter? Is the analogous result for sum 1/3^{n_k} also true, and does the proof technique extend?
